text: Build Technology Hybrid Systems Hybrid Systems Hybrid CHERI systems combine conventional pointers with explicit capabilities, supporting staged adoption while leaving some accesses outside capability protection. Replacing every pointer and binary interface at once is rarely practical. CHERI therefore supports hybrid systems, where conventional address-based software coexists with capability-aware code. Hybrid operation is a migration and experimentation tool. It is not the same security property as a pure-capability application. What “hybrid” can mean The precise model depends on the architecture and application binary interface (ABI), but hybrid software commonly has: conventional language-visible pointers for ordinary C and C++ code explicit capability-qualified pointer types for selected objects or interfaces capability registers and instructions available to capability-aware code operating-system support for saving, mapping, and passing capabilities a conventional ABI preserved for much of the program Legacy loads and stores may be authorised relative to a broader default capability or architectural context. They do not automatically carry a separate bound for each C object. Why use hybrid mode Hybrid mode can help teams: introduce one capability-aware interface at a time build protected handles and service entry points experiment with compartment mechanisms run conventional libraries while porting selected components preserve a familiar ABI during architecture development measure and debug capability operations before wider conversion It played an important role in the development of CheriBSD and the wider CHERI software model. A staged example Imagine a conventional service that receives network data. A first hybrid step might explicitly derive a bounded, read-only capability for one packet and pass it to a capability-aware parser. The parser gains useful protection for accesses through that capability. Other conventional pointers in the service remain governed by the legacy model. If the parser converts back to a conventional pointer or receives a broad default authority, the effective boundary may weaken. The security claim must therefore identify the protected path: The parser accesses packet data only through a read-only capability bounded to the packet. It should not claim: The complete service has pure-capability memory safety. ABI compatibility Keeping a conventional ABI reduces some migration costs. Existing structure layouts, pointer sizes, and call conventions may remain usable for code that does not expose capabilities. Interfaces that pass capabilities still need capability-aware calling conventions, types, relocation support, and libraries. Mixing modes is platform-specific. A library built for one ABI cannot be assumed compatible with another because both run on the same processor. Security coverage Hybrid mode provides strong enforcement where valid, tightly bounded capabilities are used. It may also support sealed objects and compartment entry mechanisms. Coverage remains selective: ordinary pointers may retain broad address-space authority compiler-created object bounds may not cover conventional code a component may still hold ambient legacy authority conversions between pointer forms require careful review This makes hybrid mode useful for transition but harder to describe with a single percentage or label. Planning a move to pure capability A hybrid prototype can identify capability-aware interfaces and porting issues. To gain broader protection: build dependencies for the pure-capability ABI replace pointer-integer assumptions fix object-bound and allocator issues validate foreign-function and assembly boundaries run the complete test suite as pure-capability code confirm that conventional fallback paths are no longer used Some systems may retain hybrid components deliberately where required. Document that residual authority and contain it behind a narrow boundary. Key takeaway Hybrid CHERI makes incremental adoption possible, but capability protection is only present where the software actually uses capabilities. For broad C and C++ pointer protection, compare Pure-Capability Systems. Where next Pure-Capability Systems A program cannot gain broad pointer protection if only a few selected pointers carry capability metadata. paragraphs: Build
Technology
Hybrid Systems
Hybrid CHERI systems combine conventional pointers with explicit capabilities, supporting staged adoption while leaving some accesses outside capability protection.
Replacing every pointer and binary interface at once is rarely practical. CHERI therefore supports hybrid systems, where conventional address-based software coexists with capability-aware code.
Hybrid operation is a migration and experimentation tool. It is not the same security property as a pure-capability application.
The precise model depends on the architecture and application binary interface (ABI), but hybrid software commonly has:
conventional language-visible pointers for ordinary C and C++ code
explicit capability-qualified pointer types for selected objects or interfaces
capability registers and instructions available to capability-aware code
operating-system support for saving, mapping, and passing capabilities
a conventional ABI preserved for much of the program
Legacy loads and stores may be authorised relative to a broader default capability or architectural context. They do not automatically carry a separate bound for each C object.
Hybrid mode can help teams:
introduce one capability-aware interface at a time
build protected handles and service entry points
experiment with compartment mechanisms
run conventional libraries while porting selected components
preserve a familiar ABI during architecture development
measure and debug capability operations before wider conversion
It played an important role in the development of CheriBSD and the wider CHERI software model.
Imagine a conventional service that receives network data. A first hybrid step might explicitly derive a bounded, read-only capability for one packet and pass it to a capability-aware parser.

The parser gains useful protection for accesses through that capability. Other conventional pointers in the service remain governed by the legacy model. If the parser converts back to a conventional pointer or receives a broad default authority, the effective boundary may weaken.
The security claim must therefore identify the protected path:
The parser accesses packet data only through a read-only capability bounded to the packet.
It should not claim:
The complete service has pure-capability memory safety.
Keeping a conventional ABI reduces some migration costs. Existing structure layouts, pointer sizes, and call conventions may remain usable for code that does not expose capabilities.

Interfaces that pass capabilities still need capability-aware calling conventions, types, relocation support, and libraries. Mixing modes is platform-specific. A library built for one ABI cannot be assumed compatible with another because both run on the same processor.
Hybrid mode provides strong enforcement where valid, tightly bounded capabilities are used. It may also support sealed objects and compartment entry mechanisms.
Coverage remains selective:
ordinary pointers may retain broad address-space authority
compiler-created object bounds may not cover conventional code
a component may still hold ambient legacy authority
conversions between pointer forms require careful review
This makes hybrid mode useful for transition but harder to describe with a single percentage or label.
A hybrid prototype can identify capability-aware interfaces and porting issues. To gain broader protection:
build dependencies for the pure-capability ABI
replace pointer-integer assumptions
fix object-bound and allocator issues
validate foreign-function and assembly boundaries
run the complete test suite as pure-capability code
confirm that conventional fallback paths are no longer used
Some systems may retain hybrid components deliberately where required. Document that residual authority and contain it behind a narrow boundary.

Hybrid CHERI makes incremental adoption possible, but capability protection is only present where the software actually uses capabilities. For broad C and C++ pointer protection, compare Pure-Capability Systems.
A program cannot gain broad pointer protection if only a few selected pointers carry capability metadata.
A pointer bug becomes dangerous when changing a number changes authority.
A media application may include millions of lines of code, dozens of libraries, and parsers for hostile input.
